sentences.text: Gryposaurus was a genus of duck-billed dinosaur with a name meaning "hooked-nosed lizard" in Greek.
This animal is distinguished from other duck-billed dinosaurs by a narrow, arching nasal hump resembling a Roman nose.
It belonged to the saurolophine hadrosaurid group, a type of duckbill dinosaur that lacked hollow head crests.
Gryposaurus was a typical-sized hadrosaurid measuring approximately 9 meters long and 4 meters high.
The distinctive nasal arch of Gryposaurus may have been used for social functions like identifying sex, species, or social ranking.
Researchers suggest the nasal arch may have been used for pushing or butting in contests, possibly flanked by inflatable air sacs for signaling.
The nasal arch likely held an air-filled skin sac used for social communication, with males possibly changing color and blood flow during mating season.
Tethyshadros was once thought to belong to the Gryposaurus genus before being described, when it was known by the nickname "Antonio".
The genus Gryposaurus is based on specimen NMC 2278, found in 1913 by George F. Sternberg in the Dinosaur Park Formation along the Red Deer River.
Lawrence Lambe described the specimen, noting the distinctive nasal arch.
The genus Gryposaurus was formally named by Lambe in 1914.
Lambe described and named Gryposaurus shortly after its discovery, highlighting its unusual nasal crest.
There are 22 recorded fossil occurrences of Gryposaurus.
Gryposaurus was a bipedal or quadrupedal herbivore that ate a variety of plants.
As a hadrosaurid, Gryposaurus was likely a herbivore that could walk on two or four legs and ate a variety of plants.
It had skull joints allowing a grinding motion and dental batteries containing hundreds of teeth, with only a few in use at once.

Gryposaurus had special skull joints allowing abrasive chewing-like movement, and its teeth were continuously replaced and packed into batteries containing hundreds of teeth, with only a handful in use at any time.
The animal likely used its wide beak to crop vegetation and cheek-like organs to hold food in its jaws.
Gryposaurus could feed on plants ranging from the ground up to about 4 meters high.
Gryposaurus' feeding range likely extended from the ground up to about 4 meters high.
Evidence suggests Gryposaurus was both a grazer and a browser, eating tough, fibrous plant material.
Gryposaurus may have preferred habitats related to rivers.
Gryposaurus may have chosen to live in areas near rivers.
Because only one specimen was analyzed, the feeding patterns inferred from its dental microwear may not represent the whole taxon.
The informal name "Hadrosauravus" was an early, unused name for the species Gryposaurus latidens.
"Hadrosauravus" is listed as a synonym of Gryposaurus but is considered a nomen nudum.
As of 2016, three named species are recognized as valid: G. notabilis, G. latidens, and G. monumentensis.
Gryposaurus lived approximately 80 to 75 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous in North America.
Gryposaurus lived between 85 and 66 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous in what is now North America.
Fossil remains of Gryposaurus have been found in the El Picacho Formation in Texas.
Argon-argon dating places the deposition of the Kaiparowits Formation between 76.1 and 74.0 million years ago.
William Parks named a skeleton Kritosaurus incurvimanus rather than Gryposaurus incurvimanus, reflecting the historical debate over whether the two genera were the same.
It is debated whether Kritosaurus is a synonym of Gryposaurus, though Kritosaurus is slightly younger.
